content: In 2014, the World Health Organization (WHO) introduced guidelines and tools for integrating reproductive health recommendations into national programs. These guidelines emphasized principles and processes for adaptation and implementation. By May 2016, WHO, in collaboration with the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS), the Global Network of Sex Work Projects, the World Bank, and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), had developed practical approaches for implementing comprehensive HIV and sexually transmitted infection (STI) programs targeting sex workers. These resources were accessible online. WHO also released consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for key populations, which were available for review as of May 2016. Additionally, UNFPA, the Global Forum on MSM & HIV, UNDP, WHO, the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), and the World Bank collaborated to create guidance for implementing HIV and STI programs for men who have sex with men (MSM). These guidelines provided practical tools for collaborative interventions. WHO published recommendations for the use of antiretroviral drugs in treating and preventing HIV infection, emphasizing a public health approach. The UNAIDS/WHO Working Group on Global HIV/AIDS and STI Surveillance also developed strategies and laboratory methods to enhance STI surveillance. WHO's regional STI focal points included experts from various regions, such as the Americas, Europe, the Western Pacific, Africa, South-East Asia, and the Eastern Mediterranean. These experts contributed to the development of guidelines for the treatment of Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The guideline development teams included specialists from WHO headquarters and regional offices, as well as external experts in reproductive health, HIV/AIDS, and STI management. The guideline development process involved reviewing existing international recommendations, including those from the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the British Association for Sexual Health and HIV (BASHH), the Public Health Agency of Canada, and other national and international organizations. Based on this review, four categories of STI conditions were prioritized for inclusion in the updated WHO guidelines. These included conditions from the 2003 WHO STI guidelines that required updates, new conditions to be added, rare conditions with limited new evidence, and conditions covered in other national guidelines but not selected for inclusion. The guideline development group (GDG) identified six priority questions for updating gonorrhea treatment recommendations. These questions were framed using the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) format. For example, the treatment of uncomplicated genital and anorectal gonococcal infections in adults and adolescents was evaluated, comparing single and dual therapy regimens. Critical outcomes included microbiological cure, clinical cure, STI complications, antimicrobial resistance, and side effects. The evidence review process involved systematic searches for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomized studies. The search strategies were developed by trained information specialists and included key terms based on the PICO questions. The evidence was analyzed to determine the benefits, harms, feasibility, and acceptability of interventions. Priority was given to interventions with high ratings for critical outcomes, such as microbiological cure and compliance. The updated guidelines also addressed treatment failure of gonorrhea to cephalosporins, treatment of neonatal ophthalmia, and prevention of neonatal ophthalmia.
